analysis.one_liner: Requires banks to reimburse customers tricked by scams into sending electronic payments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in August 2024, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, if a scammer tricks you into authorizing a payment yourself — a fake IRS call, a romance scam, a phony Zelle transfer — federal law generally treats that as an 'authorized' transfer, and the bank does not have to make you whole. This bill would change the Electronic Fund Transfer Act so that payments you were tricked into sending are treated the same as transfers a thief made without your knowledge: your bank would have to reimburse you, and the bank that received the money would have to share the loss. It would also expand what counts as a billable 'error' your bank must fix, such as money stuck in a frozen account or goods billed but never delivered.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who are defrauded into authorizing electronic transfers — scam victims on payment apps and bank transfers — who would be reimbursed instead of eating the loss, and all account holders who gain clearer rights when money is frozen or goods are billed but never delivered.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines 'unauthorized' transfers under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to include transfers the consumer initiated because their authorization was 'fraudulently induced,' placing scam-induced payments under the same reimbursement rules as outright theft [S2].

Requires the consumer's financial institution to reimburse the consumer for unauthorized or fraudulently induced transfers, and splits the resulting loss evenly between the bank holding the consumer's account and the bank that received the money, so the receiving institution has skin in the game in blocking scam proceeds [S2].

Adds to the definition of 'error' a consumer's inability to access funds in a frozen, closed, or otherwise inaccessible account (except where required by court order or law enforcement), and charges on statements for goods not accepted or not delivered, obligating banks to investigate and resolve these disputes [S2].
Places the burden on the financial institution to show a transfer was authorized or not fraudulently induced, rather than on the consumer [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions that facilitate electronic transfers would bear the cost of reimbursing scam losses and of compliance and dispute-resolution systems; some of those costs could be passed back to customers through fees or tighter fraud screening that adds friction for everyone.

drawbacks.text: The bill puts the loss on financial institutions even when the consumer was careless or the facts are disputed, which could invite false claims and difficult judgment calls about what counts as 'fraudulently induced' [S2].
Banks could respond by adding friction — longer holds, more verification steps, higher fees — or by refusing to serve customers they deem fraud-prone, imposing costs on ordinary users [S2].

Loss-sharing with the receiving institution could fall hardest on smaller banks and credit unions that lack large fraud departments, and the Consumer Bureau would need to write new rules to sort out who 'materially supports' transfers before the liability regime could work as intended [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is direct: money stolen through scams today is largely unrecoverable, and this bill would shift that loss to the institutions best positioned to detect and stop it. The costs are real but manageable — banks already run fraud-detection systems, and loss-sharing gives receiving banks an incentive to block scam proceeds at the source. The main design risk is disputes over which claims are genuine, which the rulemaking process would have to resolve.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in early August 2024 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat with no hearing, markup, or vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, killing it automatically.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters, the senior Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the bill on August 2, 2024 [S1].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S3].

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day it was introduced, and the recorded action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, credit unions, and payment providers are better off because the bill died: they keep the current system in which scam-induced 'authorized' transfers are the customer's loss, and they face no shared liability with receiving institutions.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.role: U.S. Representative (CA-43), sponsor; senior Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Protecting Consumers From Payment Scams Act and assigned it to the Financial Services Committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the recorded action history shows nothing after the referral [S4].

against.name: Banking and payments industry
against.role: Banks, credit unions, and peer-to-peer payment providers facing new reimbursement and loss-sharing liability
against.what_they_did: The industry has broadly opposed extending mandatory fraud reimbursement to payments consumers were tricked into authorizing, since such rules shift scam losses onto institutions; no opposition activity appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member — a Democrat — sponsored the bill and no one cosponsored it, and no votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape of the fight never formed in the record.

industries.note: The bill would require consumer-account institutions to reimburse customers for scam-induced transfers and to share those losses with the receiving bank, moving a cost currently borne by defrauded customers onto institutions. Institutions' interest here runs against scam victims', who would otherwise recover nothing [S2].

industries.industry: Payment providers and receiving institutions (including peer-to-peer networks and money transmitters)
industries.note: By defining 'financial institution' to include anyone providing means of access to transfers, and by splitting liability with the institution that receives a fraudulent transfer, the bill would make payment intermediaries financially responsible for scam proceeds flowing through their rails. This gives them a direct financial stake in blocking scams that today they can largely ignore [S2].
